clue.text: Spooner’s jittery poor style of swimming

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of word pairs, so his name tells us to swap the starts of the two words given by 'jittery' and 'poor'

blocks.note: jittery people are tense; take the opening sound from the next word
broke means penniless; swap its opening sound with the first word's

explanation.surface: A nervous, weak swimmer thrashing about in the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: STRESSED BROKE with the openings exchanged becomes BRESSED STROKE, which is said just like BREASTSTROKE.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaststroke is one of the standard competitive swimming techniques, done face down with a frog kick.

clue.text: Happen upon sources of inspiration for puzzles

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting upon another means it comes first, above the second

blocks.note: to be is to exist or take place
the Muses were the Greek goddesses who inspired artists

explanation.surface: Someone who gets the ideas for their puzzles by chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puzzles' reads as a plural noun beside 'inspiration'; it is really the verb, and 'Happen' is not 'come across' but simply BE.
explanation.definitionFit: To bemuse someone is to confuse or bewilder them, a straight verb synonym.

clue.text: Serious pests uncovered beneath net

indicators.note: in a down clue, what sits beneath comes second, so the pests follow the net
stripping the covers off a word removes its outside letters, keeping the middle

blocks.note: to net money is to earn it
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Troublesome insects lurking under a garden net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Net' looks like a noun, a mesh over the pests; it is the verb meaning to take home as profit.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest describes someone sincere and grave in manner, a plain adjective synonym for serious.

clue.text: Regret splitting stone with one’s turning bladed tool

indicators.note: one word splitting another pushes itself into the middle of it
'with' simply puts the next piece alongside the first
turning the whole assembly round makes it read backwards

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for the stone, a British weight of 14 pounds
to rue is to regret
an ace is a one in cards, so one's reads as ace's

explanation.surface: Someone sorry for grinding a blade on a whetstone.
explanation.walkthrough: The turn applies to the whole assembly, not just 'one's', so build everything first and reverse at the end. A stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Secateurs are pruning shears, a gardener's hand cutter with two short blades.

clue.text: Give pound to expand loot

indicators.note: the pound goes inside the loot word and so makes it bigger

blocks.note: to sack a town is to plunder it
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: An instruction to hand over money so a stash of stolen goods grows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' looks like a verb opening an instruction; it is the noun, the looseness in a rope. 'Loot' is likewise a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Slack in a rope or schedule is the amount of looseness or play, which is also called give.

clue.text: Register to keep old farm animal

indicators.note: a word that keeps another holds it inside itself

blocks.note: a roster is a list or register of names on duty
O is a standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A farmer keeping a record of an elderly beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Register' looks like a verb, to record something; it is the noun, a list of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a cockerel, the male domestic chicken kept in a farmyard, so an example of the category.

clue.text: One worshipped rakish rogue tackling knight

indicators.note: a rogue version of a word has gone wild, its letters out of order
tackling someone means wrapping your arms round them, so the rearranged letters surround the knight

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A dashing scoundrel bringing down a knight, whom somebody adores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rakish rogue' reads as one dashing villain, but 'rakish' is the fodder and 'rogue' the instruction to scramble it.
explanation.definitionFit: Krishna is a major Hindu god, an avatar of Vishnu, revered by millions of devotees.

clue.text: I enchant with sound playing classical composition

indicators.note: the letters are played about with, set in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A performer boasting that their playing casts a spell on listeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only joins the two lots of fodder; 'sound playing' tempts as a phrase about music, and it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Chanson de Nuit is a short piece by Elgar for violin and piano, a work in the classical repertoire.

clue.text: Plants perhaps beneath tender meaty fare

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece beneath comes second, so the plants follow the tender

blocks.note: one who tends a flock, with the possessive S
a plant is a planted informer, an example of a spy, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: Vegetables served under soft, juicy meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The split is SHEPHERD'S + SPIES: the S does double duty in the letters, since plants give SPIES and the tender gives SHEPHERD. 'Tender' looks like an adjective for meat; it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Shepherd's pie is minced lamb baked under mashed potato, a classic British dish of meat.

clue.text: Poet’s in Italy in church

indicators.note: Italy is placed inside the church, so the church letters surround it

blocks.note: someone who is in is at home
RC is Roman Catholic, a church abbreviation
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A statement that a poet lives in Italy, perhaps in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's' looks like 'poet is'; it is the possessive, which an adjective can replace. The first 'in' must be read as a word in its own right, giving HOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Homeric means belonging to Homer, the ancient Greek epic writer, so it stands for that writer's.

clue.text: Axe I lump around to cut wood

indicators.note: turning the pair around makes the letters run backwards
a piece that cuts a word goes into it, splitting it in two

blocks.note: used as it stands
a lob is an old and dialect word for a lump
ash is a tree and its timber

explanation.surface: A woodcutter hauling a heavy axe round to chop timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axe' sits among 'cut' and 'wood' as a tool; it is the verb meaning to scrap.
explanation.definitionFit: To axe a scheme or job is to get rid of it entirely, the same as abolishing it.

clue.text: Deft carrying very big weight – it’s unproblematic

indicators.note: the word for deft carries the others inside it

blocks.note: a neat move is deft and skilful
OS is outsize, the clothing label for very big
W is an abbreviation for weight

explanation.surface: A skilled lifter hoisting a huge weight and calling it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: OS, for outsize, is a clothing label for very large sizes, and the weightlifting surface hides that 'Deft' is the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: No sweat is an informal idiom said of a task that causes no difficulty at all.

clue.text: Mixing this sauce, son and I might supply soup kitchen

indicators.note: mixing the sauce's letters with the extras stirs them into a new order
the son and the I are the extras added to the sauce, so they are what to strike from the result

blocks.note: the eleven letters the whole mix produces
take these letters out of the phrase
take this letter out too; what remains is the fodder

explanation.surface: A cook making a sauce with his son for a charity kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus SON and I rearranges to SOUP KITCHEN, so work back by removing SON and I from that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Ketchup is the tomato condiment, and 'this sauce' points to the answer word as the sauce in question.

clue.text: Attack playing series of games

blocks.note: a show that is on is playing
a set in tennis is a series of games

explanation.surface: A tennis player going on the offensive during a set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attack' reads as a verb for the player; it is a noun, an older sense of the answer beside 'start'.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is an assault or onslaught, an older noun sense alongside beginning.

clue.text: Direction of return for Phoenix, a state capital

blocks.note: the phoenix is reborn from its ashes and rises again, heading skyward
a and per both mean 'for each', as in ten pounds a head
a case is a state of affairs

explanation.surface: Road directions for someone heading back to Phoenix, the capital of Arizona.
explanation.walkthrough: Phoenix really is a state capital, which hides both the mythical bird and the letter sense of 'capital'.
explanation.definitionFit: A capital letter is an upper-case letter, the printers' term from the top type tray.

clue.text: Uninitiated osteopath’s in trouble immediately

indicators.note: without an initial means the word loses its first letter
letters in trouble are in disarray, out of their proper order

blocks.note: the word minus its first letter
the S of the possessive joins the fodder

explanation.surface: An unqualified back doctor who needs to get out of a mess fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uninitiated' reads as untrained; here it strips the osteopath of its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Posthaste is an adverb meaning with great speed, from the old urgent instruction on mail.

clue.text: Aristos charge to catch game

indicators.note: the charge word catches the game, holding it within

blocks.note: dues are a fee or charge
chess is a board game

explanation.surface: Wealthy landowners charging at a shoot to bag some pheasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' in a surface about aristocrats suggests grouse and pheasant; it is a board game.
explanation.definitionFit: Duchesses are women of high noble rank, and aristos is informal for aristocrats, so these are examples.

clue.text: Cold scrap for American’s pudding

blocks.note: C is cold, as on a tap
a rumble is US slang for a street fight or scrap

explanation.surface: Leftover cold scraps given as dessert to a visitor from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a leftover morsel; here it is a fight. A crumble is fruit baked under a buttery topping.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumble is a British baked dessert of fruit under a rubbed flour and butter crust, so a type of sweet course.

clue.text: Designate European ship to protect inlet

indicators.note: the ship shields the inlet by enclosing it

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
Noah's ark was a ship
an arm of the sea is an inlet

explanation.surface: Naming a European warship to guard a bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Protect' puts the inlet inside the ship, the usual way a container is signalled by guarding or shielding.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark funds or items is to set them aside for a particular purpose, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Floated along with foot lifted out no longer wet

indicators.note: the foot is lifted out of the word, so its letters are removed

blocks.note: to drift is to float along on a current
ft is the abbreviation for foot

explanation.surface: A swimmer floating with a foot raised from the water until dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' seems to belong to the swimmer; it is the abbreviation FT, taken out of the floating word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried describes something whose moisture has gone, which is the plain meaning of that phrase.

clue.text: Played from start for Dundee United

indicators.note: the start of the named club's first word supplies one letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the place name
united nations are allied ones

explanation.surface: A footballer who has been in the side from the outset for a Scottish club.
explanation.walkthrough: Dundee United is a real Scottish football club, which makes 'Played' look like a match report; it means toyed or trifled.
explanation.definitionFit: To dally is to trifle or toy with something idly, so a past tense verb synonym for amused oneself.

clue.text: Adapting plans, this figure might be single parent

indicators.note: adapting the combined letters means reworking them into a new order

blocks.note: the twelve letters the whole mix produces
take these letters out of the phrase; what remains is the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone raising a child alone, having to change their plans.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus PLANS rearranges to SINGLE PARENT, so remove PLANS from that phrase and unscramble the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An integer is a whole number, one kind of numerical figure, and 'this' points at the answer word.

clue.text: This dull dorm converted could be ultramodern

indicators.note: a converted building has been remade, just as the letters are rearranged
the dormitory is the extra added to the dull word, so its letters are the ones to strike from the result

blocks.note: the eleven letters the whole mix produces
take these letters out of the word; what remains is the fodder

explanation.surface: A drab student dormitory given a sleek, modern makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer plus DORM rearranges to ULTRAMODERN, so take DORM out of that word and sort what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Neutral colours are beige and grey, lacking brightness, so the adjective suits a drab look.

clue.text: Woman partial to sparkLY DIAmonds

indicators.note: only part of the following words is taken, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: runs across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A woman who loves glittering jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partial to' reads as 'fond of', which suits the surface; it also says a part of the words is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Lydia is a female given name, so this is one example of a woman.

clue.text: Fifty brought in to handle work for summit

indicators.note: fifty is brought into the handle word, going inside it

blocks.note: a hilt is the handle of a sword
L is the Roman numeral fifty
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Fifty staff called in to deal with the job of a leaders' meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summit' suggests a meeting of leaders; it is the top of a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: A hilltop is the highest point of a hill, and a summit is the peak of any height.

clue.text: Engineer at centre drilled audibly within vessel

indicators.note: the centre of an eight-letter word is its two middle letters
audibly means we want what the word sounds like, not its spelling

blocks.note: the fourth and fifth of its eight letters
to bore a hole is to drill it; the two sound alike in British speech

explanation.surface: An engineer drilling a hole in the middle of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like the person doing the drilling; only its middle two letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Inboard describes something located inside a ship's hull, like an inboard motor.

clue.text: Polish hosts ultimately offering full board

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letters of the words that follow
to host is to take in guests, so the polish word holds the letters inside

blocks.note: to shine shoes is to polish them
the last letter of each word

explanation.surface: A Polish landlord who gives guests full board in a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' carries its capital from the start of the clue, suggesting the nationality; it is the verb. 'Full board' is a hotel term for all meals, but only 'board' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle is a thin wooden tile used for roofing, so a kind of flat timber board.

clue.text: Office accessory needs returning, object chewed by pet

indicators.note: returning sends the needs word back the way it came
something chewed is in the pet's mouth, so the pet word surrounds it

blocks.note: pet and dear are both terms of endearment
to need something is to lack it
an end is an aim or object

explanation.surface: A dog gnawing things around the office that the owner needs back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' reads as a thing the pet chews; it is a purpose or aim. Only 'needs' is turned round, not the object.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk calendar is a small date planner that sits on office furniture, one kind of workplace item.
